sections.h2: Where is Milford, CT, and what makes it a shoreline city?
sections.html:
Milford is a coastal city in New Haven County, between New Haven and Bridgeport. It had 50,558 residents in the 2020 census and covers about 25 square miles, of which more than 3 square miles is water.

Wikipedia says Milford has over 14 miles of shoreline on Long Island Sound, the most of any town in Connecticut. Much of that shoreline forms Silver Sands State Park, and Charles Island is part of the park and a protected bird nesting ground. A sandbar to the island is walkable at low tide, though the page warns the tide change has led to drownings.

The city includes the village of Devon, at the mouth of the Housatonic River near Stratford, and the borough of Woodmont. That coastal setting shapes what buyers ask about when they look at a Milford house.

sections.h2: What is the history of Milford?
sections.html:
English colonists tied to the New Haven Colony bought the land from Ansantawae, chief of the local Paugusset, on February 1, 1639. They called the area Wepawaug, after the small river that runs through it, and built a grist mill on that river in 1640.

Over time Milford gave rise to several other towns. Woodbridge split off in 1784, Orange in 1822, and West Haven later came from Orange in 1921. The remaining Milford was known for shipbuilding, farming and oystering, and in the late 1800s it became a beach resort for people from New Haven and Bridgeport.

The Borough of Woodmont was incorporated in 1903, and the Town of Milford, including Woodmont, became a city in 1959. Interstate 95 through Milford was completed in 1958, and the Connecticut Post Mall followed in the 1960s and 1970s.

One oddity affects old land records: starting in 1902, Quaker Oats boxes carried coupons for deeds to tiny lots in a never-built Liberty Park subdivision. Town officials ended those lots in the mid-1970s through a general foreclosure. It is a good example of why title searches matter.

sections.h2: What beach and neighborhood areas does Milford have?
sections.html:
Milford is divided into many named communities, and several are on the water. Wikipedia lists Downtown Milford, Devon, Rivercliff, and a string of beach communities including Walnut Beach, Wildermere Beach, Laurel Beach, Point Beach, Bayview and Morningside.

Six of these are chartered by Special Act of the General Assembly and have some municipal powers, including taxing authority. Woodmont is a borough with all statutory municipal powers while remaining part of the city. That detail matters if you sell in one of these areas.

  • Ask whether your property is in a borough, beach association or chartered community.
  • Ask whether that body charges taxes or fees in addition to the city bill.
  • Ask the city which tax collector bills for your address.

The city has five public beaches with lifeguards for residents: Gulf Beach, Anchor Beach, Hawley Avenue Beach, Walnut Beach and Middle Beach, along with seven private beaches.

sections.h2: Who are the largest employers in Milford?
sections.html:
Schools, a consumer products maker, the city, a hospital campus and manufacturers lead the list. The city's 2025 annual financial report, as summarized on Wikipedia, ranks the Board of Education first.

Doctor's Associates, the company behind the Subway chain, was also once headquartered here, according to Wikipedia. Milford's mix of local jobs and commuter access to New Haven, Bridgeport and New York keeps demand for housing steady, though we do not publish price estimates on this page.

sections.h2: How do you travel in and out of Milford?
sections.html:
Interstate 95 and U.S. Route 1 cross the southern part of Milford, and the Wilbur Cross Parkway crosses the northern part. The Milford Parkway, also called the Daniel S. Wasson Connector, links the parkway to I-95 and Route 1.

  • The Metro-North New Haven Line has a Milford station downtown with direct service to New York City.
  • The Milford Transit District runs in-town service.
  • Connections are available to Greater Bridgeport Transit, Norwalk Transit District and CT Transit New Haven.

Rail and highway access draw commuters. Many sellers mention a long commute as the reason for moving, so a convenient address is something to describe truthfully when you talk to a buyer.

Milford Public Schools runs eight elementary schools, three middle schools, two high schools and an alternative education high school. The two main high schools are Jonathan Law High School and Joseph A. Foran High School.

Middle schools are East Shore, Harborside and West Shore. Elementary schools include Calf Pen Meadow, John F. Kennedy, Live Oaks, Mathewson, Meadowside, Orange Avenue, Orchard Hills and Pumpkin Delight. Private options include Lauralton Hall, St. Mary School and Milford Christian Academy. School assignments change, so verify with the district.

sections.h2: How do Milford's tax office and city government work?
sections.html:
Milford's Tax Collector collects real estate, motor vehicle and personal property taxes, plus sewer use fees, sewer assessments and sewer laterals. Collection is based on a Grand List certified each October 1 by the Assessor's Office.

The Board of Aldermen sets the mill rate through the adopted city budget, and the Sewer Commission sets the sewer use fee. The city says it cannot override Connecticut statutes. Government is a mayor and Board of Aldermen, with a separate Planning and Zoning Board handling land use and development.

  • Tax Collector: 70 West River Street, First Floor, Room 105.
  • Mailing address: PO Box 3025, Milford, CT 06460-0825.
  • Phone 203-783-3217, open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., except holidays.
  • The office also offers a tax calculator and a mill rate history page.

sections.h2: What does a Milford seller pay when the deed is recorded?
sections.html:
The seller pays Connecticut's conveyance tax at recording. Under C.G.S. 12-494, a typical home sale carries 0.75 percent for the state and 0.25 percent for the city, and the state portion rises above $800,000 on a residential estate.

The state requires Form OP-236 to be filed with the town clerk, and the clerk may not record a deed until the tax has been paid. Sales of a principal residence in lieu of foreclosure and some defective-foundation sales have separate exemptions.

A short sale case is covered too. The state exempts a principal residence if the price is too low to cover the mortgages and the priority tax and sewer liens, so a seller in that spot should ask an attorney.

sections.h2: What do Milford sellers usually face?
sections.html:
Milford sellers often include owners of older beach cottages, families settling an estate, and landlords with multi-unit buildings. A coastal house can have maintenance needs that buyers worry about, and lenders may look closely at flood zone status.

A listing means repairs, showings and a financing contingency. An as-is cash sale skips those steps. You can compare both and keep whichever one fits your timeline.

  • Gather tax bills, sewer bills and any association invoices.
  • Check for beach association or borough charges.
  • Confirm who holds title and whether an estate is involved.

faqs.q: How much shoreline does Milford, CT have?
faqs.a: Milford has over 14 miles of shoreline on Long Island Sound, which Wikipedia describes as the most of any Connecticut town. Much of it is part of Silver Sands State Park.

faqs.q: Do beach communities in Milford tax separately?
faqs.a: Some do. Six Milford communities are chartered by Special Act and have taxing authority, and Woodmont is a borough with full municipal powers. Ask whether your address falls inside one.

faqs.q: Where is the Milford tax collector?
faqs.a: The office is at 70 West River Street, First Floor, Room 105. The phone number is 203-783-3217, and hours are Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
The Board of Aldermen sets it through the adopted city budget, and taxes are based on the Grand List each October 1. The Sewer Commission sets sewer use fees.

faqs.q: Who pays the conveyance tax in Milford?
faqs.a: The seller pays it when the deed is recorded. On a standard home sale it is 0.75 percent to the state and 0.25 percent to the city, with a higher state rate above $800,000.
